nameStory: The Mottled Prominent gets its name from the beautiful mottled or speckled pattern across its wings, which looks like someone dabbed different shades of brown and gray paint with a sponge. The word 'prominent' refers to the distinctive tufts of scales that stick up from the moth's back when at rest, giving it a fuzzy, almost punk-rock appearance that makes it stand out from other moths.
description: The Mottled Prominent is a medium-sized moth with intricate brown, gray, and tan patterns that create excellent camouflage against tree bark. When resting during the day, it holds its wings in a tent-like position over its body, with those characteristic scale tufts creating bumps along its back. These moths are part of the prominent moth family, known for their cryptic coloring and unusual resting postures. Adults typically have a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches.

idTips.label: Mottled Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Wings display a complex mix of brown, gray, and tan patches that look like bark camouflage, with wavy lines and irregular spots that feel rough to the touch due to dense scaling

idTips.label: Prominent Scale Tufts
idTips.description: Distinctive fuzzy tufts of scales stick up from the thorax and abdomen when at rest, creating a bumpy profile that you can feel if you gently touch a resting moth

idTips.label: Tent-like Resting Pose
idTips.description: Holds wings in a steep, roof-like angle over the body when resting on tree trunks, rather than spreading them flat like many other moths

idTips.label: Thick, Fuzzy Body
idTips.description: Body appears robust and densely covered in soft, hair-like scales that give it a woolly texture when touched gently

idTips.label: Bark-matching Coloration
idTips.description: Overall coloring perfectly matches the mottled grays and browns of tree bark, making them nearly invisible when pressed against trunks during daylight hours

habitat: Look for Mottled Prominents in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially areas with oak, maple, and birch trees where their caterpillars feed. They're commonly found resting on tree trunks during the day in both mature forests and woodland edges. You might also spot them at porch lights or other artificial lights at night, particularly in wooded residential areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically May, when you might find them resting on tree bark during warm days or attracted to lights on mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time occurs through June and July when adults are most active and commonly seen at lights. Look for caterpillars feeding on deciduous tree leaves during this period.
seasonality.fall: A second generation may appear in late summer to early fall, with adults flying through September. Caterpillars prepare for winter by pupating in soil or leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae buried in soil or hidden under leaf litter, with no visible adult activity during the cold months.

funFact: When threatened, Mottled Prominent caterpillars can actually shoot their own poop up to 6 feet away as a defense mechanism, earning them the nickname 'bombardier caterpillars' - it's one of nature's most unusual ways to say 'leave me alone!'
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other prominent moths in the family, but the Mottled Prominent's combination of very bumpy scale tufts and intricate bark-like mottling sets it apart. Remember: if it looks like a piece of bark grew fuzzy bumps, you've likely found a Mottled Prominent.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'prominent' can be confusing since it doesn't refer to the moth being large or obvious, but rather to those distinctive protruding tufts of scales that create bumps along the moth's profile when viewed from the side.
compareHints: As the only Macrurocampa species in New England, compare it with other prominent moths like the White-dotted Prominent or Variable Oakleaf Caterpillar Moth. The Mottled Prominent stands out with its particularly complex mottled pattern and very pronounced scale tufts, while other prominents tend to have simpler patterns or less obvious bumps along their backs.
